all_scored.summary: Large language models are increasingly deployed as LLM-as-a-Service (LLMaaS), where user queries are sent to remote LLMs for inference, raising severe privacy concerns about the exposure of sensitive user inputs. Differentially private inference mitigates these risks by injecting noise into input embeddings. However, existing methods struggle to balance privacy and utility, as stronger privacy protection often leads to substantial accuracy degradation in LLM inference. In this work, we propose DP-SPD, a differentially private LLM inference framework that protects user queries by hiding the real query among client-generated dummy queries. All queries are randomly shuffled before being sent to the server, preventing direct identification of the user's true intent. To improve inference efficiency, we exploit the shared-prefix structure among queries and reuse transformer key--value (KV) caches during decoding. We analyze the privacy guarantee of DP-SPD and evaluate its utility on classification and generation tasks, as well as its privacy protection under QIA, EIA, and GPT-based attacks. Experimental results show that our method achieves strong inference-time privacy protection and near-plaintext utility while improving inference efficiency through shared-prefix KV-cache reuse.

all_scored.title: GNetSS: Towards Learning GNSS Corrections without Ground Truth
all_scored.summary: We present GNetSS, a self-supervised GNSS position correction framework that improves the robustness of single point positioning (SPP) without requiring ground-truth locations for training. GNetSS combines a transformer-based network with a deterministic differentiable positioning solver. The network predicts satellite-wise pseudorange corrections by modelling inter-satellite geometry and temporal context, while the solver converts these corrected measurements into receiver position corrections under GNSS geometry and optional motion constraints. Unlike supervised GNSS correction methods that rely on ground-truth, GNetSS derives its training signal directly from GNSS measurement consistency. Experimental results show that GNetSS improves robustness across open-sky, urban, and forested environments. The method is particularly effective at suppressing large-error outliers, reducing the maximum 3D positioning error by over 50% compared with SPP. These results demonstrate the potential of self-supervised pseudorange correction for scalable and robust GNSS positioning in real-world autonomy applications. Code and the in-house dataset will be released upon acceptance.

all_scored.title: GPU-Accelerated Secure Inference for Drug--Target Interaction Prediction
all_scored.summary: Deep learning models that predict drug--target interactions (DTI) can speed up drug discovery, but the candidate drugs they score are valuable intellectual property that their owners cannot reveal. Secure multiparty computation (MPC) lets two servers compute a prediction on a secret-shared drug, without either server learning the drug. However, secure inference of deep models is slow. Non-linear operations require communication between the servers, and MPC arithmetic does not map naturally to GPUs. In this paper, we present our solution to Track~III of the iDASH 2026 privacy and security competition, which asked for fast two-party secure DTI inference on GPUs. Our solution is built on the co-design of MPC-friendly models and MPC protocols. On the model side, we design SlimDTA, a DTI model that reduces the operations on the secret drug, and in particular the non-linear operations that require communication. On the protocol side, we build a GPU framework that evaluates the linear layers with additive secret sharing and the non-linear layers with function secret sharing, including a custom CUDA kernel for the comparisons. Our solution won first place in the competition, at under 10,ms per prediction on average, and its secure predictions match the plaintext model to within 0.02%.

all_scored.title: GRODE-RTL: Source-Mapped Dependency Views for LLM-Based RTL Repair
all_scored.summary: Large Language Models show great potential for automated Register-Transfer Level repair, yet they struggle with non-local faults where root causes and failing outputs reside far apart in source code. Treating RTL as a flat token sequence obscures hardware dataflows, whereas exposing complete synthesized graphs overwhelms the model with fine-grained metadata. To resolve this representation dilemma, we propose GRODE-RTL, an anchor-centric representation that extracts the single-clock-stage fan-in cone of a suspect register from the netlist, maps netlist nodes back to editable source lines, and organizes them into a compact hop-partitioned dependency view. By prioritizing direct drivers and folding distant hops, GRODE-RTL guides standard tool-using agents without exposing ground-truth hints or oracle feedback. We evaluate GRODE-RTL across 30 formally validated non-local faults using three LLMs (DeepSeek-V4-Flash, GLM-5.2, and MiniMax-M3) alongside a controlled six-configuration ablation study. GRODE-RTL improves pass@1 over source-level exploration by 16.7% on DeepSeek, by 26.7% on GLM-5.2, and by 20.0% on MiniMax-M3, with consistent gains on the hard-to-retrieve far-distance and indirect-anchor subsets of all three models. Our controls isolate structural relevance from generic context expansion, proving that selective dependency organization rather than full graph exposure is key to effective RTL repair.

all_scored.title: ColorRef: Calibrating Verbal Feedback for Color Revision
all_scored.summary: People rarely specify an exact color when asking someone to revise a design: they might say \textit{a little darker} or \textit{more blue} after seeing a proposal. A language-model assistant must then infer not only which way to change the color, but how far. We study this distinction with \textsc{ColorRef}, a color reference game in which a model guesses a color from a description and a teacher, knowing a recorded target hidden from the guesser, supplies verbal corrections. On 1{,}000 crowd-sourced description--target pairs, three rounds of deterministic oracle feedback reduce mean target distance from 42.33 to 22.15 $ΔE_{76}$. However, those corrections provide additional information, and improvement alone does not establish well-calibrated feedback following. A controlled Qwen3-14B diagnostic reveals a more specific failure: following a requested direction and ordering graded phrases do not guarantee a suitable step size; strong modifiers can induce excessive changes. We therefore measure each receiver's typical response to \textit{a little}, \textit{somewhat}, and \textit{much} on separate colors and select wording matched to its observed steps. On 128 held-out starting colors, calibration reduces one-step mean error from 12.36 to 6.86 for Qwen3-14B and from 11.06 to 5.89 for Gemma 4 12B against a fixed graded-wording rule. The benefit is concentrated on large corrections, with many unchanged cases and no consistent increase in threshold success. Our findings show that following the direction of feedback is not the same as making an appropriately sized revision.

all_scored.title: Extending Rademacher Complexity-Based Generalization Theory to Domain Generalization
all_scored.summary: Domain generalization (DG) aims to train models on multiple source domains with distinct distributions to ensure robust performance on unseen target domains. In doing so, it elevates the concept of generalization from the traditional sample level to the distribution level. Existing theoretical frameworks introduce a domain space endowed with a meta-distribution to extend classical generalization analysis to this new setting. However, these approaches typically treat the domain space as devoid of geometry. In reality, the domain space is an inherently infinite-dimensional, nonlinear abstract space composed of probability distributions, and its complex geometric properties fundamentally determine generalization behavior. Consequently, existing geometry-free theories of domain generalization have a fundamental limitation. They lack a formal characterization of what distinguishes distribution-level generalization from sample-level generalization, leaving the inherent difficulty of generalizing across domains largely unexplained. To bridge this gap, we formalize the domain space as the Wasserstein space over the representation space. Building on the geometric properties of this space (specifically the $\mathrm{CD}(K,\infty)$ curvature theory) we derive a novel, geometry-dependent DG error bound. By introducing an additional curvature-dependent confidence term, this bound formally disentangles the two levels of generalization effects and reveals the essential nature that domain generalization is affected by both the invariance and the curvature of the representation space. Finally, we experimentally validate the effect of curvature on domain generalization.

all_scored.title: TRAC: Efficient Diffusion Language Models for Machine Translation via Length-Aware Decoding
all_scored.summary: Machine translation with large language models requires both high translation quality and low generation latency. Accelerating translation while preserving quality is therefore essential for practical deployment. Diffusion large language models (dLLMs) can generate tokens at arbitrary target positions through iterative denoising, offering a new paradigm for parallel translation beyond sequential autoregressive decoding. However, existing methods still incur redundant computation: fixed target generation lengths waste computation on unused positions, while confidence-only commitment delays medium-confidence tokens whose predictions have largely stabilized. To address these issues, we propose TRAC, a training-free adaptive decoding method for diffusion machine translation. TRAC adapts the target generation length using source length and translation direction, with a conservative fallback to the maximum length for empty or unusually short outputs. It preserves high-confidence commitment while identifying temporally stable medium-confidence tokens for early commitment using cross-step top-1 persistence and approximate Jensen-Shannon divergence over Top-$K$ distributions. On bidirectional Chinese-English translation across FLORES-200, WMT23, and NTREX-128, TRAC reduces model forward calls by 24.9% to 36.8% and achieves sentence-level generation speedups of 1.91 to 2.19 times over Fast-dLLM, with only a 0.02-point decrease in macro-average COMET. These results demonstrate that adaptive generation lengths and stability-aware token commitment improve the efficiency of diffusion machine translation.

all_scored.title: Erasing the Wrong Thing: Conditional Attribute Leakage and Concept Erasure in Shared Foundation-Model Embeddings
all_scored.summary: Medical-image embeddings are increasingly shared in place of raw images for authorized downstream tasks, yet they may reveal sensitive attributes. Standard concept-erasure methods target population-level guardedness. However, we prove that, when binary task and sensitive labels are associated, global and task-conditional linear guardedness cannot both hold while a nonzero linear task signal is preserved, so global erasure must either eliminate that signal or retain task-conditional linear leakage. We further show how global erasure affects linear readers' discrimination between positive and negative samples with different sensitive attributes, deriving an approximate closed-form prediction of its utility cost from pre-erasure statistics. Motivated by this conflict, we introduce Task-Conditional LEACE (TC-LEACE), a closed-form variant of LEACE that enforces linear guardedness within each task stratum of its fitting data. We evaluate four vision foundation models on 85 CelebA attribute pairs spanning a broad range of associations. After LEACE, conditional leakage persists across all four encoders, the discrepancy between marginal and conditional audits increases with association strength, and predicted utility costs track observed losses. We then examine hospital chest radiographs using three foundation models, including two biomedical models, in which chest-tube status is strongly associated with diagnosis. Although a marginal attack on LEACE-erased embeddings underperforms a diagnosis-only reference, chest-tube status remains detectable within diagnosis strata. TC-LEACE recovers most of LEACE's linear task-utility loss while keeping task-conditional leakage within a prespecified margin of LEACE's.

all_scored.title: AesDistill: Distilling Generative Aesthetics for Image Color Enhancement
all_scored.summary: Image color enhancement aims to improve visual appeal, but previous methods often learn to reproduce ground-truth expert targets. These targets reflect the preferences of a few experts and cover a limited range of aesthetic choices. Matching them does not ensure stronger aesthetic quality across different tastes and scenes. By contrast, large generative models learn rich visual knowledge from large image collections and often produce vivid, appealing image edits. However, direct generation can change the source image's semantic structure along with its colors. In this paper, we introduce AesDistill, a framework for distilling generative aesthetics into image color enhancement. We use 4 leading open-source large generative models to produce 64,644 edited images as teacher targets at a cost of about 3,360 H100 GPU-hours, forming the AesDistill Dataset. AesDistill also includes AesDistill Student, a 1.13M-parameter model that learns teacher color changes through confidence-weighted supervision while preserving the source image's semantic structure. We evaluate AesDistill with 12 aesthetic and 4 image-quality assessment models. Every teacher's targets rank above the FiveK and PPR10K expert target means in the joint assessment. Across both datasets, AesDistill Student outperforms all 20 baseline methods and ranks directly behind the 4 teachers. These results demonstrate that distilling aesthetics from generative models enables a compact student to outperform methods trained on expert targets.

all_scored.title: Physical Laws without Physics Loss? Probing Learned Dynamics in Video World Models through Forced Response
all_scored.summary: Do video world models learn physical laws without a physics loss, or merely imitate motion? Overall motion and appearance scores cannot settle it. We investigate this through nonlinear forced response: an excitation shakes the support of a suspended object. We introduce dual visual-numeric conditioning and adapt six image-to-video backbones to predict this motion using only the flow-matching loss. Wan predicts motion accurately and generalizes to unseen excitations, objects, poses, and scenes. Counterfactual tests suggest capabilities beyond replaying training videos. But what laws have they learned? We design three tiers of tests using Taylor expansions of the dynamics and geometry. All six reproduce the linear response, including resonance; five capture higher-order dynamics, including nonlinear softening. Remarkably, softening is barely present in training: only 0.74% of the swing's squared displacement. Extensions to a double pendulum and a rocking block show sustained dynamics are learned more faithfully than brief impacts. Yet learned dynamics may fail to appear when state estimation or propagation goes wrong. We turn these tests and findings into strategies to improve video training and generation.

all_scored.title: QUBO-based feature selection for MRI undersampling pattern design
all_scored.summary: We formulate undersampling mask design for Cartesian magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) as a feature subset selection problem. Each sampling line is represented by a binary feature indicating whether it is included in each candidate mask. Using candidate masks and their training-set evaluations, we estimate mutual information (MI) and conditional mutual information (CMI). These estimates and a sampling-count penalty define a quadratic unconstrained binary optimization (QUBO) model. The model is solved using simulated annealing and quantum annealing to determine a feature subset and its corresponding sampling mask. We assess the selected subsets on the test set through zero-filled reconstruction in Fourier undersampling simulations using fastMRI knee magnitude reference images, with patient-disjoint training and test sets. At all six tested target sampling rates from 15% to 40%, the resulting reconstructions have lower mean root mean square error than those obtained with four conventional sampling methods. They also have higher mean structural similarity than those obtained using univariate mutual-information ranking at all tested rates. These results support information-theoretic feature selection as an approach to MRI undersampling mask design under the tested zero-filled simulation settings.

all_scored.title: Deviations from the NTK Regime in CNNs under Joint Depth-Width Scaling
all_scored.summary: The concentration and training-time constancy of the neural tangent kernel (NTK) depend on the interplay between network width, depth, and initialization. While joint depth-width scaling has been studied in fully-connected, residual, and recurrent networks, its effects in convolutional neural networks (CNNs) remain less understood. We investigate these effects numerically in CNNs, examining NTK dispersion at initialization and kernel rotation during training. Let depth $L$ be the number of convolutional layers, and width $C$ the number of channels per layer. We find that NTK dispersion increases with $L/C$ in the critical and chaotic initialization regimes, but remains small in the ordered regime. At critical initialization, dispersion curves approximately collapse as a function of $L/C$, suggesting a nontrivial joint scaling regime. During training, kernel rotation generally increases with $L/C$, even in the ordered regime where initial dispersion is small. Together, these results suggest that $L/C$ may govern NTK deviations from the infinite-width limit in certain regimes, and that NTK concentration at initialization and stability during training exhibit different scaling behaviors.

all_scored.title: DAWN: Robust Neural Blind Deconvolution via Alternating Wiener Guidance
all_scored.summary: Blind image deconvolution (BID) is an ill-posed inverse problem that aims to jointly recover a sharp image and blur kernel from a single degraded observation. Under nontrivial and high noise, which is common in photography and scientific imaging such as microscopy, BID remains particularly challenging, as existing methods suffer from noise overfitting and inaccurate kernel estimation. Existing training-data-free learning methods for BID, such as those based on the deep image prior (DIP), often utilize external guidance by including model-based estimates as additional loss terms, which underexploits the information these estimates carry especially under nontrivial noise. To address these challenges, we propose DAWN, a training-data-free DIP framework that alternates between injecting model-based estimates directly into the model input and refining this imperfect estimate with the network's own prior. To provide more reliable kernel estimates for these injections, we apply autoencoding regularization to both the image and kernel networks. On natural and scientific images under varying levels of Gaussian and Poisson noise, DAWN outperforms state-of-the-art methods in both image and kernel quality (achieving up to +4.5 dB over the next best baseline on the Levin dataset at $σ= 0.1$). Without any training images, DAWN remains highly competitive with a state-of-the-art diffusion model on FFHQ, despite the latter being trained on a massive number of in-distribution images.

all_scored.title: Splice-Core: Low-Order-Bit-Splicing GEMM for Highly Energy-Efficient AI Inference Accelerators
all_scored.summary: Splice-Core is a temporal-unary/binary (tub) hybrid general matrix multiplication (GEMM) unit that minimizes low-order accumulation latency, while retaining value-dependent execution for high-order activation bits. We present two novel processing element (PE) variants: (i) Splice-BP utilizing bit planes, and (ii) Splice-LUT, which selects a shared weight multiple in a single cycle. Compared to a binary systolic array, Splice-BP/Splice-LUT achieve 77.4%/76.4% geometric-mean tile energy reductions, respectively, across 26 INT4 convolutional neural network (CNN) and large language model (LLM) workloads in 45nm. Splice-LUT further increases geometric-mean tile throughput by 44.4% and reduces geometric-mean energy-delay product (EDP) by 6.13x across the 26 configurations. Across the evaluated W8A8 convolution and expert-projection workloads, Splice-BP and Splice-LUT reduce tile energy by 77.3-88.1%. Post-place-and-route INT4 yields 14%/9% smaller area for Splice-BP/Splice-LUT, compared to the systolic array.

all_scored.title: Can an LLM Fix a Language Model Without Training It?
all_scored.summary: Although an external language model can select and test repairs to another model's weights, behavior can also be recovered through fixed numerical edits. We assessed the value of interactive selection in a controlled study of Transformer repair. After inspecting predictions, activation summaries, and weight statistics, the editor selects projection recipes to apply to the target without gradient updates. We analyzed 20 recorded sessions involving five masked and causal language models, comparing the selected edits with fixed projections, scripted and matched-budget black-box search, and low-rank adaptation. Under the core two-layer fault, live selection matches black-box search on SmolLM2 and Qwen2.5. For Pythia, live selection achieves 65.62% completion accuracy, compared with 0% for black-box search and 66.15% for a fixed projection. Under a separate compound fault affecting attention and feed-forward weights, both scripted and LLM-guided selection increase the descriptive five-checkpoint mean from 24.89% to 71.25% using the same operator family. On unmodified checkpoints, scripted projection yields small gains or losses on a separate set of framed questions. The experiments identify cases in which feedback changes an edit decision, operator coverage accounts for recovery, or supervised adaptation performs better. Combined with measurements of parameter restoration and preservation, these comparisons establish the scope of controller-guided repair for the tested faults and completion tasks.

all_scored.title: PSTO: A PDE-structured transport operator with shared implicit updates for multiscale CDR systems
all_scored.summary: Multiscale convection-diffusion-reaction (CDR) systems couple spatial transport with local stiff reaction kinetics, making their numerical simulation computationally demanding. Conventional neural surrogates require costly coupled CDR training data, and their parameter counts scale with the number of transported variables, limiting scalability to high-dimensional CDR systems. Here we propose a PDE-Structured Transport Operator (PSTO) that learns convection--diffusion dynamics solely from reaction-free data. By embedding the PDE structure into the neural architecture, PSTO generalizes to full CDR systems at inference without retraining. A single transport operator block is shared across all transported variables and refined through relaxed fixed-point iterations, performing an implicit-like correction in latent space. This improves stability during recursive multi-step prediction without adding trainable parameters. We evaluate PSTO on three benchmarks: a canonical 2D CDR system, a multiscale Robertson counterflow flame, and a multiscale hydrogen planar jet flame. In every case, PSTO reduces the mean relative $L_2$ error after 100 coupled steps by at least 50% compared to the strongest neural baseline. Ablation studies on the fixed-point iterations and detailed error decomposition further confirm that PSTO achieves both high one-step accuracy and long-term stability in coupled rollouts. Time-step sensitivity analysis shows that PSTO maintains accuracy even with a tenfold larger time step, whereas baseline accuracies decay rapidly as the time step increases. This framework enables efficient, modular modeling of multiscale CDR dynamics by separating transport learning from the treatment of local kinetics.

all_scored.title: Generative News Recommendation Reproduces Popularity: A Memorization-Based Analysis
all_scored.summary: Text-based generative recommenders can go beyond ranking existing items by directly generating item titles or other textual representations. In the news domain, this raises a societal concern that models may repeatedly surface already popular articles and thereby narrow the diversity of information to which users are exposed. We investigate training-data memorization as one mechanism behind this concentration. Using approximately 20 million browsing sessions from a Japanese news service, we continually trained an instruction-tuned Llama 3 8B model to generate the next article title in a session. The generated-title distribution was more concentrated and less diverse than the distribution of titles observed in the browsing logs. Frequently repeated target titles exhibited greater verbatim and approximate memorization, and more strongly memorized titles were generated in response to a wider range of prompts. These findings support a pathway in which popularity in behavioral logs becomes repeated training text, is preferentially memorized, and is subsequently reproduced by a generative recommender. An exploratory target-level deduplication condition reduced both memorization and output concentration, while substantially reducing the training-set size and recommendation accuracy. Our results suggest that popularity bias in generative recommendation may arise not only from user preferences or ranking objectives, but also from the model's tendency to reproduce frequently encountered strings, with important implications for information diversity on news platforms.

all_scored.title: Copilot or Culprit? How AI Is Changing Open-Source Bug Reporting and Maintenance
all_scored.summary: AI-generated bug reports have drawn criticism for unreliable claims and faulty reproducers that burden maintainers. However, as LLM capabilities improve, some maintainers have begun to express more positive views on AI use in bug reporting and maintenance. Understanding this evolution requires examining whether AI-involved reports are becoming more reliable, which uses of AI are associated with valid findings, and how maintainers investigate these reports and act on them. To this end, we conduct the first large-scale study of 120,918 bug reports from 101 open-source projects between January 2024 and September 2026, tracing AI involvement from discovery and reporting through validation and resolution. Our findings show that AI-involved reports become more complete over time, with a growing share of reports confirmed as valid. In bug reporting, AI for reproduction and diagnosis are associated with higher validity, whereas report writing is not. Extends into maintenance, maintainers increasingly use AI to investigate code and recommend fixes. However, they devote more effort to AI-assisted reports of human-discovered bugs than to reports of AI-discovered bugs. These findings highlight both AI's growing participation in bug investigation and the continuing need for verification and follow-up. Drawing on these findings, we provide practical guidance for turning AI-generated findings into verifiable reports: emphasizing reproducibility, verification, and accountability. We followed this guidance when submitting 53 reports on AI-discovered bugs, of which 69.81% were accepted by maintainers as of writing.

all_scored.title: PAD: Policy-Aware Data Valuation for Autonomous Driving
all_scored.summary: End-to-end autonomous driving increasingly depends on scaling training demonstrations, yet data growth does not guarantee proportional gains. However, additional data do not guarantee better policies: a demonstration that benefits one planner may be redundant or harmful to another. Existing curation methods typically infer data value from intrinsic sample properties or training-dependent proxies that do not measure downstream policy utility. To address this, we introduce \textbf{Policy-Aware Data Valuation (PAD)}, a framework that assigns each candidate demonstration a utility specific to the target driving policy. PAD combines scene-level calibration feedback with projected policy gradients and a regularized approximation of local training geometry, producing scalable influence-based values for the policy. A controlled group-removal study establishes the directional fidelity of these values, while cross-planner analysis shows that the same candidate pool induces markedly different rankings across planner families. On DiffusionDrive, PAD improves EPDMS over real-only training by $3.5$ points on NavTest and $5.0$ points on NavHard. Policy-specific curation consistently outperforms real-only and full-pool training across diffusion-, regression-, and flow-matching-based planners while substantially reducing scene-level regressions. These results establish policy-aware data valuation as a basis for replacing indiscriminate data accumulation with targeted policy improvement, enabling more efficient and reliable scaling of autonomous-driving systems.

all_scored.title: On the Informativeness of Structural Stability Bounds for GNNs: GINs versus GATs
all_scored.summary: Stability bounds for graph neural networks limit how much node representations can drift when the graph changes, but they are rarely compared with the simplest alternative: a bound on the distance between any two outputs, whatever the graph. We derive structural stability bounds for Graph Isomorphism Networks (GINs) and single-head GATv1 networks under deterministic edge perturbations that need not be small, and compare each with such a perturbation-independent diameter bound. For GINs, we characterize exactly when the stability bound is tighter, through a condition linking perturbation size, depth and maximum degree; it holds with a wide margin on Cora, but fails beyond a few layers on the low-degree MUTAG graphs. For GATv1, the bound is never tighter, which calls for analyses based on attention masses.

all_scored.title: Tether: Verified Stateful Policy Engine for System-Level Monitoring of Agents
all_scored.summary: Autonomous AI agents are increasingly deployed for long-running tasks that execute arbitrary shell commands or programs. However, these actions can result in unauthorized network requests or persistent, malicious changes to the user's file system, processes, or privileges. Existing defense mechanisms rely on either LLM-based monitors, which lack provable safety guarantees, or stateless policy enforcement layers, which miss multi-step data flows and execution side-effects unmodeled by the policy language (e.g., network calls initiated inside a Python script). We introduce Tether, a framework for runtime enforcement of stateful security policies over the observed side-effects of an agent's actions. Tether executes each proposed action in an ephemeral, isolated sandbox, inferring abstract action semantics from observed system calls. Tether then enforces stateful policies over these inferred semantics, permitting actions to proceed only if they comply with the policy. Policies and action semantics are defined in an embedded DSL in Lean 4 capable of expressing diverse constraints, including information flow control (IFC), access control, and network security policies. Because actions can propagate labels from sources to destinations, a single rule can enforce fine-grained IFC policies across multi-step execution flows of arbitrary length. Expressing policies in Lean enables formal verification that they satisfy global security invariants (e.g., preventing network access after reading a sensitive file). We evaluate Tether on realistic coding-agent benchmarks across both benign and adversarial trajectories. With a single policy shared across all tasks, Tether blocks 100% of in-scope attacks while maintaining a benign false-positive rate under 5%.

all_scored.title: Bradley-Terry Training Can Distort Outcome Probabilities of Initially Accurate Language World Models
all_scored.summary: Comparative feedback, in which a judge says which of two candidate outcomes is closer to what happened, is a practical way to train language world models that assign probabilities to an action's outcomes. We show that, fitted with a Bradley-Terry objective, it need not teach the true outcome probabilities and can distort accurate ones. On a simulated robot push with enumerated outcome distributions, this objective takes a model that is accurate on unseen layouts (hazard error 2.4 percentage points, pp) and moves 33 to 43 pp of its probability onto outcomes that none of a condition's enumerated branches produces. The cause is the objective, not the comparisons: its optimum, computed before training, predicts where the model ends up, and a likelihood that knows the judge's rule learns from the same comparisons without the shift. The shift is robust: it recurs on unseen conditions, under five candidate laws and a three-fold denser enumeration, and about 29 pp remain without the physically impossible events. Its cost is conditional: with those events it inflates hazard probabilities, and a threshold inherited from the pre-feedback model costs about 3 pp of utility per decision on trained and 1 to 2 pp on unseen conditions, through false rejects; without them the utility loss averages below 1 pp over six seeds, though a small regret in action choice remains. Audits of readout, response and decision trace the effect from probabilities to actions.

all_scored.title: From Data Alignment to Parameter Generation: Few-Shot Cross-City Traffic Prediction with Conditional Diffusion
all_scored.summary: Accurate mobile traffic forecasting is crucial for network service management, supporting proactive capacity provisioning, congestion mitigation, and energy-efficient operation. However, many cities and regions are data-scarce (e.g., newly deployed or poorly instrumented areas), thus making traffic prediction a few-shot learning problem and limiting the practicality of standard data-driven models. Existing cross-city solutions primarily rely on data-space alignment to match traffic distributions between data-rich and data-scarce cities, but such alignment is often brittle under real-world distribution shifts, measurement noise, and city-specific bias. To address these limitations, we propose a Conditional Diffusion-based Parameter Generation (CDPG) framework. Instead of aligning raw data, CDPG learns the conditional distribution of high-performing predictor parameters for source cities and directly generates node-specific model parameters for the target city. To support reliable adaptation for network traffic prediction, CDPG conditions parameter generation on multi-modal spatio-temporal context. Specifically, CDPG captures spatial environment cues by combining satellite imagery with large language model (LLM)-derived semantic descriptions, and summarizes complex temporal behaviors via unsupervised pattern clustering. These contextual components guide CDPG in producing parameters tailored to each base station's operational context, thereby improving robustness under cross-city and cross-region shifts. Extensive experiments on three large-scale datasets show that CDPG consistently outperforms state-of-the-art cross-city few-shot baselines by up to 9.72% on standard forecasting metrics and remains robust for few-shot multi-step prediction. The code is available at https://github.com/LingoodBoy/CDPG.

all_scored.title: Measuring Hallucination in Large Language Models for Cyber Threat Intelligence: An Exploratory Study
all_scored.summary: Large language models (LLMs) are increasingly used in cyber threat intelligence (CTI) tasks, such as summarization and question answering. However, they may produce hallucinations, false or misleading content not grounded in the source text, which can mislead analysts and corrupt downstream security decisions. This paper presents an exploratory measurement study of hallucinations in LLM-based CTI. We introduce HalluVision, a reproducible framework that generates LLM outputs, extracts domain-specific entities using a fine-tuned named entity recognition model, and evaluates factual consistency using multiple similarity metrics. Using 4,940 real-world cybersecurity articles, we measure hallucinations in outputs from two commercial LLMs and one open-weight LLM. Measurements are validated against 100 human-annotated outputs and two established faithfulness detectors. Results show that semantic similarity aligns with human judgments, whereas entity-based metrics exhibit limited agreement. Differences between models are concentrated in question answering, while entity extraction quality limits what entity-level metrics can reveal.

all_scored.title: An Explainable and Scalable Hierarchical Tensor Framework for Integrating Multi-Omics and Digital Pathomics
all_scored.summary: Background: Precision oncology requires integration of heterogeneous molecular and pathology data, yet many fusion models offer limited biologically grounded interpretability and struggle with missing modalities. Methods: We present Hierarchical Interpretable Tensor Fusion (HIT-Fuse), integrating six modalities: somatic copy number variation, DNA methylation, RNA sequencing, microRNA expression, RPPA protein abundance, and vision transformer-derived pathomics across four TCGA cohorts (glioma, lung adenocarcinoma, breast, and kidney cancer). Modality-specific autoencoders compress high-dimensional inputs, followed by two-stage CP tensor decomposition. Missing latent modalities are reconstructed using clinical covariates and observed omics to expand cohorts and retrain downstream models. A mathematical traceback mechanism enables global and local xAI attributions. Results: HIT-Fuse identifies distinct latent subgroups with significant survival stratification in glioma, breast, and kidney cohorts, both with complete and reconstructed modalities. Cohort expansion yields cohort-specific gains, including a 56.4% relative increase in weighted F1 for glioma. Biological validation against DepMap CRISPR screens, miRTarBase and RPPA annotations supports decoded drivers across all four cohorts. Essential gene rates range from 6.2% in glioma to 7.6% in lung cancer; example drivers include ANAPC11, SNRPD1, PLK1 and RPL14. Of decoded miRNAs, 71-92% have miRTarBase regulatory support, while 77-84% of selected genes are covered in DepMap. Conclusions: HIT-Fuse combines hierarchical tensor fusion, missing-modality reconstruction and traceable attributions to support interpretable multi-omics and digital pathology-based cancer prognosis across heterogeneous cohorts.

all_scored.title: FlashX: Scaling Robotic Experience Reuse for Embodied Agents with CBA-Based NAND Flash
all_scored.summary: Embodied agents are emerging as a promising paradigm for complex robotic tasks, leveraging Vision-Language-Action (VLA) and World Action Models (WAMs) to generate actions through Diffusion Transformer (DiT)-based iterative denoising. However, existing models often struggle to generalize to out-of-distribution (OOD) environments. We observe that retrieving successful experiences and using them to warm-start denoising enables agents to better adapt to unfamiliar situations while reducing computational overhead. This creates a new opportunity to improve task accuracy and inference efficiency simultaneously, in contrast to conventional acceleration techniques that trade accuracy for computation. However, realizing this opportunity requires scaling experience banks, introducing substantial storage and search overhead that challenges the capacity, bandwidth, and power constraints of edge systems. We propose FlashX, a CMOS Directly Bonded to Array (CBA)-based NAND flash architecture for scalable experience reuse in embodied agents. FlashX exploits CBA's high internal bandwidth for parallel pSLC key search, employing interleaved Compute-in-Flash (CIF) engines to sustain sensing throughput while retaining dense TLC latent storage. Proprioception-aware clustering further reduces search overhead and enables incremental experience acquisition without global reclustering. Evaluations across VLA and WAM workloads demonstrate up to 12.24\%p and 7.43\%p improvements in task success under dense and compute-efficient configurations, respectively. FlashX achieves 2.57$\times$ higher search throughput than the strongest prior NAND search architecture under pSLC sensing, with a further 9.7$\times$ search reduction through clustering. This delivers 1.29--3.95$\times$ end-to-end speedup and 1.12--2.34$\times$ energy efficiency improvement over SSD-based retrieval.

all_scored.title: Efficient Multimodal Agents for Auditing 3D Worlds
all_scored.summary: Multimodal agents can now build interactive 3D worlds and games, yet these worlds, like those built by people, often contain glitches such as floating objects, walls that can be walked through, or objects that change when no one is looking. An automatic auditor could check such worlds at scale and provide rewards for agents that build them, but only if it is both accurate and cheap. Auditing requires three abilities, namely navigating to the objects that may contain a glitch, triggering glitches that appear only after a specific behavior, and recognizing what is wrong. Current auditors are either accurate but slow and expensive or cheap but unreliable. We study how much of the audit small models can take on. A 4B vision language model fine-tuned end to end on verified trajectories of a frontier teacher guided by Bayesian search learns to navigate and trigger, and six such explorers together match a frontier model on both, but recognition stays far behind. We therefore build an auditor in which a swarm of small explorers navigates and triggers, and a frontier model reviews what they record and report. On WorldAuditBench, our auditor succeeds on 55.9% of 213 tasks in Unreal Engine 5 and Three.js worlds, 13.6 points above the strongest auditor reported, at less than a quarter of its cost. It matches the frontier reviewer exploring on its own at 4.6 times lower cost and about half the latency. Without further training, it also answers embodied questions about real-world scans, matching the frontier reviewer exploring on its own and surpassing four other frontier models by 6.4 to 16.6 points.

all_scored.title: Dynamics of Protected State Evolution
all_scored.summary: States with identical protected observations can admit different future interventions. Each transition specifies its successor, response increment, required initial reserve and net consumption. Composing these records in execution order distinguishes protocols with equal net consumption and different initial reserve requirements. At a fixed state, a weighted Gram operator determines the linear response ellipsoid and a quotient identifies directions attainable only through cooperation between blocks. Nonlinear systems with identical complete affine data can have incomparable finite-budget response sets. In regular charts, the first correction to quadratic minimum cost is a covariant cubic form involving the third derivative of cost and the Hessians of protection and response. At singular gates, sequential feasibility depends on the peak reserve along the path. A history-weighted operator detects responses outside the old channel's range closure. Controlled congruence characterizes exact reductions of deterministic labelled dynamics, and a two-cut value identity separates the effect of paid verification from that of subsequent action selection. On Qwen2.5-7B Base, two projected policies preserved 2,048 reference top tokens under a per-position KL ceiling of $2\times10^{-5}$. Over 200 arrivals they recovered 391 of 396 initial rejections. Each yielded over 1,200 times the held-out cross-entropy reduction of historical-channel-only AdamW. Under an expanded 2,560-position contract, fixed continuation and neutral renewal began on the same protected logit fiber in distinct structural strata. Both admitted all 200 subsequent writes. Fixed continuation yielded 1.74 times the held-out loss reduction per unit squared write cost. Renewal had a smaller KL excess on the first candidate tested at every arrival and used fewer full verification scans.

all_scored.title: COVERAGE-TRACE: Source-Side Counterfactual Tracing for Detecting Omissions in LLM Summaries
all_scored.summary: Omissions are difficult to verify because missing information leaves no output span to inspect: a summary may be factually supported while still excluding a decision, qualification, quantity, or condition needed to preserve the source's meaning. We introduce COVERAGE-TRACE, a source-side counterfactual framework that evaluates omission as dependence on a designated atomic source fact. It replaces only the target fact with type-matched alternatives, holds the candidate summary fixed, and measures the resulting change in its teacher-forced, length-normalized likelihood. A summary covering the target should respond more strongly than one omitting it, while aggregation across multiple counterfactuals reduces sensitivity to replacement choice. We evaluate COVERAGE-TRACE on 80 matched covered--omitted QMSum pairs spanning several fact types and four open-weight models. Multi-CF achieves 0.764--0.825 AUROC, compared with 0.640 for the strongest evaluated text-only baseline. On Falcon-7B, targeted interventions achieve 0.779 AUROC, whereas shuffling counterfactual assignments reduces performance to 0.533; target deletion is effective while unrelated deletion is not. However, adjustment for meaning-preserving paraphrases reduces AUROC to 0.591--0.624. COVERAGE-TRACE therefore provides a practical, complementary signal of target-specific source--summary dependence, but not a wording-invariant semantic coverage probability. These results establish source-side intervention as a promising approach to omission detection while identifying semantic invariance as the central remaining challenge.

all_scored.title: Differentially Private Score Estimation with Applications to Score-Based Generative Models
all_scored.summary: Estimating the score function of a distribution plays a central role in statistics and machine learning, with applications in distribution estimation, sampling, and score-based generative modeling. However, learning scores from sensitive data raises privacy concerns. These concerns are particularly pronounced in score-based generative modeling, where trained models may memorize individual training examples and expose sensitive information through membership inference and data extraction attacks. Although non-private score estimation has been extensively studied, the statistical limits of its private counterpart remain less understood. In this work, we study score estimation under $(α,β)$-differential privacy for $d$-dimensional sub-Gaussian distributions with locally $γ$-Hölder-continuous scores. We develop a sampling-based private score estimator using quadratic B-splines and the exponential mechanism, and we implement our proposal through projected Langevin Monte Carlo with runtime polynomial in the sample size $n$. The proposed estimator satisfies $(α,β)$-differential privacy, and achieves expected density-weighted squared error $\mbox{polylog}(n) \max(n^{-2γ/(d+2γ+2)},\,(nα)^{-2γ/(d+γ+1)})$. We also establish a nearly matching private minimax lower bound, thereby characterizing the privacy-accuracy trade-off for score estimation. As an application, we construct a differentially private diffusion model whose privacy guarantee is independent of the number of denoising steps. We show that, with an appropriate discretization scheme, the resulting diffusion model attains nearly minimax optimal expected total variation error among all private distribution estimators. We validate our theoretical findings through experiments on both synthetic and real-world datasets.

all_scored.title: Keystone: Judging Previews at Key Steps for Test-Time Search in Diffusion Models
all_scored.summary: Text-to-image diffusion and flow models yield a preview, their clean-image estimate, at every denoising step. When they miscount, drop or misplace objects, test-time search is in a bind: its verifiers are reward models built for finished images, so judging early misreads blurry previews, and judging late, as best-of-N does, pays to fully denoise doomed candidates. We find that the image is not the problem: the outcome is settled as denoising starts, by the seed or by a stochastic sampler's first steps, and already shows in early previews; what fails on them is the judge, as reward models read them near chance on several kinds of prompts. We introduce Keystone, a training-free judge of previews that compiles a prompt into typed questions about its objects, counts, colours and positions and has an off-the-shelf multimodal decision model answer them. Asked this way, the judge reads counts and positions from early previews better than reward models read them from finished images. Searching at these key steps on GenEval with SD3.5-Medium, Keystone's adaptive search and pruning significantly outperform best-of-8 with every other verifier at under half its generator compute, and as a drop-in verifier there, the Keystone score significantly improves best-of-N, progressive seed pruning and FK steering; without retuning, both searches stay significantly above the strongest other verifier's best-of-N on average over four base models and three benchmarks. Keystone thus moves test-time judgment to the key steps where the outcome already shows.

all_scored.title: MATE: Mobile Agent Trustworthy Execution for Safe and Efficient Mobile Control
all_scored.summary: Mobile agents on personal smartphones can affect private data, payments, settings, and the foreground screen. We present MATE (Mobile Agent Trustworthy Execution), an execution-layer system that controls the boundary between agent action proposals and device effects without modifying the underlying model. MATE represents each UI primitive as a structured action record that combines the instruction, target app, screen context, primitive, and action fields. Runtime Guardrail (RG) maps this record to an allow, block, or user-approval decision; Predefined Task Routing (PTR) serves recurring requests through verified routes with post-execution screen checks; and a floating interface keeps execution in a compact overlay. On MobileSafetyBench, MATE raises high-risk blocking from 29.7% to 97.0% under GPT-4o. On AndroidWorld, it reduces LLM calls by up to 6x and raises recurring-use task success to 95.7%.

all_scored.title: When and why can integral constraints improve the accuracy of physics-informed neural networks?
all_scored.summary: Adding constraints obtained by integrating governing equations to the loss has been reported to improve the accuracy of physics-informed neural networks (PINNs) in several applications, but mathematical understanding of these benefits remains limited. For several partial differential equations (PDEs), we derive stability estimates for losses with and without integral constraints. The comparison reveals that in certain parameter regimes, the standard loss has very weak control over specific error components, and that the integral constraints restore uniform control of these components. This explains when and why the constraints improve accuracy. Finally, numerical experiments support this interpretation. In parameter regimes where the standard loss is predicted to have weak control over those components, the two losses indeed show clear differences in accuracy. Conversely, in regimes where the standard loss retains sufficient control, both losses yield similar accuracy.

all_scored.title: Sequential Probability Assignment against Smoothed Adversaries with Unknown Base Measure
all_scored.summary: Smoothed online learning has recently been studied as a way to bypass hardness results for the fully adversarial setting, which can be overly pessimistic. In this framework, the adversary is constrained to generate contexts from distributions having a bounded density with respect to some fixed base measure $μ$. Prior work makes the strong assumption that $μ$ is known to the learner, with notable exceptions including Block et al. (2024) and Blanchard (2025). In this paper, we study sequential probability assignment (a.k.a., online learning with log loss) with smooth, well-specified data in the more general setting where $μ$ is \emph{unknown}, without the Lipschitz condition imposed in the work of Block et al. (2024) and Blanchard (2025). We prove regret upper bounds against both adaptive and oblivious smoothed adversaries: the adaptive bound is controlled by empirical $\ell_\infty$ Hellinger entropy, while the oblivious bound improves this dependence to empirical $\ell_2$ Hellinger entropy, the notion that has been shown to characterize the complexity of learning with i.i.d. data (Bilodeau et al., 2023). Both bounds are obtained through algorithms based on truncated empirical Hellinger covers. We complement these results with a general lower bound, showing that our upper bounds are essentially tight for some natural classes, which implies a separation in the difficulty of smoothed online learning between regimes where $μ$ is known and where it is unknown.

all_scored.title: Mesh-Free Keypoint Learning for Category-Level 6D Object Pose Estimation
all_scored.summary: Category-level 6D pose estimation relates partial RGB-D observations of unseen instances to a canonical frame shared across a category. Object-aware reconstruction helps adaptive keypoints retain the geometry of the visible surface. Common reconstruction targets select observed points by their distance to a registered instance surface. We present MORSEPose, which derives this support directly from standard pose and metric-size annotations. We map observed 3D points to normalized object coordinates and retain those inside a tolerancedilated pose-and-size envelope. This construction is consistent across camera frames and metric scales. When the annotated extent bounds the object surface, the envelope conservatively contains the support of a conventional surface-distance selector. We integrate this target with multi-level RGB-D features, adaptive keypoints, and learnable category context. Experiments on REAL275 and HouseCat6D show that the envelope closely matches surface-based supervision at both point and task levels, remains stable under boundary perturbations and viewpoint changes, and supports competitive category-level pose accuracy across benchmarks.

all_scored.title: Persona Lenses: What Makes a Vision-Language Model See Through Its Persona's Eyes?
all_scored.summary: Vision-language models have been used to simulate where a user looks on a web page. However, a persona in the prompt reaches the simulated gaze only partly. We measure this reach as the difference in one model's gaze between two MatrAIx personas that differ in a single attribute. We introduce persona lenses, which place the persona between the model and the page: a text lens (a two-step prompt in which the model first writes what the persona would look at), a pixel lens (marks on the region matching the persona's interests) and a weight lens (a dwell reward gated to keep the scanpath natural). Using Qwen3-VL (4B and 32B) and Qwen3.5-9B on generated and live pages, we compare the lenses with one another and with scale, the 32B model with no lens. It has been confirmed that the text lens separates the personas strongly but is not robust to profile changes that should not move gaze. The pixel lens separates the personas less but is unaffected by attributes unrelated to gaze. At 4B and 9B, the weight lens separates the personas on interests held out from training, with no extra step on a new page. The 32B model separates the personas with the base prompt alone. Therefore, the choice of a lens depends on cost and model size.

all_scored.title: Joint Language Modeling for In-the-Wild Speech-Scene Generation with Distinct Token Representations
all_scored.summary: Speech-scene generation aims to synthesize intelligible target speech together with diverse environmental sounds as a coherent acoustic scene. The task is considered challenging in two respects. Speech and environmental audio differ substantially in their semantic and acoustic characteristics, yet existing approaches typically model the complete scene using a single mixed acoustic representation. At the same time, the two sounds are closely related in real-world speech scenes, whereas conventional approaches usually rely on simulated scenes mixed from independently recorded sources. We propose a large language model (LLM)-based framework for joint modeling of distinct speech and environment token streams. A source-aware neural audio codec extracts temporally aligned speech and environment tokens from mixed audio, and a pretrained LLM generates both token streams in an interleaved fashion conditioned on the natural-language scene description and speech content. This formulation preserves source-specific representations while modeling the token streams within a shared generative context. Since both streams are extracted directly from mixed recordings, the model can also be adapted to in-the-wild speech scenes without isolated sources. Our experimental results demonstrate that the proposed framework improves speech intelligibility, scene relevance, and audio quality over existing speech-scene generation techniques, with consistent gains from real-world adaptation. We further investigate the effects of distinct token representations and interleaved generation, and analyze whether the environmental sound remains stable while speech is active and how the two streams interact.

all_scored.title: Coordinated Use of Large Language Models in Academic Research
all_scored.summary: This study proposes a methodological framework for the coordinated use of multiple large language models in academic research. Its central argument is that involving more models does not in itself guarantee more reliable results; what matters is how cognitive and verification operations are organised. The framework is based on seven principles (procedural independence, functional allocation, the diagnostic value of divergence, the diagnostic value of convergence, external verification, proportionality of checking, and human epistemic responsibility) and sets out a non-linear multi-LLM protocol in which independently obtained results are compared, critically examined and, where necessary, verified against external sources. The approach is illustrated through real-world cases drawn from research practice. The study concludes that moving from a single language model to a coordinated multi-LLM process represents a change in the organisation of research, in which the researcher makes the final decisions and bears scholarly responsibility.

all_scored.title: AIstatLab at BraTS-GoAT 2026 Task 3: Quality-Controlled Consensus Pseudo-Labeling and Dense Expert Adaptation
all_scored.summary: BraTS-GoAT Task 3 evaluates brain-tumor segmentation across heterogeneous entities using shared ET, TC, and WT regions. We present a 3D ResidualEncoderUNet trained with quality-controlled consensus pseudo-labels, a training-only nested-region objective, and a four-expert bottleneck adapter. Five-fold ResEnc-M/L teachers gener ated predictions for 1,138 unlabeled cases; fusion, hierarchy enforcement, and confidence-and-agreement screening retained 983 for training with 1,351 annotated cases. The final five-fold ResEnc-M entry achieved mean DSC 0.834, mean NSD 0.510, and Acalc = 0.6720 on the validation server. Component effects were modest and region-dependent, with the clearest gains on ET. Source code is available at https://github.com/HeeSeung-Shin/Brats2026-Goat-HS.

all_scored.title: WeightCode: Installing New Capabilities into Neural Networks via Weight-Space Programming
all_scored.summary: Neural networks encode learned capabilities in their weights, yet extending those capabilities with explicit task knowledge remains a fundamental challenge. Here we show that Weight-Space Programming (WSP), in which executable programs read, construct or modify a network's weights directly, can install new capabilities within trained neural networks. WeightCode, a WSP framework, uses a frozen language model to write executable weight programs that install new computations into trained neural networks using task knowledge and their existing weights, without gradient-based training. Once installed, the new capabilities run independently of the language model. Given a grammar or eight demonstrations, weight programs enable previously unseen command compositions (0% to 99.8% exact match) and a new pickup action (0% to 98.4% success), while preserving the original command and navigation capabilities. On ImageNet, four weight programs achieve net gains of 8.84-17.62 points while preserving clean accuracy, outperforming the best of eight fine-tuning methods under matched examples, checks, and retention constraints. In a Vision Transformer, causal interventions show that installed noise-correction gates drive robustness gains, while their selective activation preserves clean accuracy. Rerun on five independently trained Vision Transformers without further language model calls, ten weight programs retain 83-110% of their source-network gains on average, whereas copying their fixed weight edits yields negligible gains. Six programs written for an already edited network add 5.23-14.50 points of contrast robustness while retaining the previously installed noise gain. Together, these results establish WSP as a new route to acquiring and accumulating capabilities in trained neural networks through reusable weight programs.

all_scored.title: TuringPAI: A Foundation for On-Device Physical AI
all_scored.summary: Physical AI requires models that understand spatial relationships and dynamic environments and translate observations into actions under limited onboard compute. We present TuringPAI, a family of models for on-device Physical AI comprising TuringPAI-VL for shared vision-language understanding, TuringPAI-Drive for autonomous driving, and TuringPAI-Embodied for robotic manipulation. TuringPAI-VL is a 0.65B model built on HybridViT-MLQ, which combines convolutional local aggregation with Transformer-based global modeling. Multi-scale Latent Queries integrate spatial features and observation history within the same visual Transformer, providing a compact, structured interface to the language model. Training combines general vision-language data with geometric, cross-view, and temporal supervision. TuringPAI-VL supports general multimodal understanding and improves quantitative geometric perception over Qwen2-VL-2B, while providing a shared initialization for the two downstream VLA models. For autonomous driving, TuringPAI-Drive maintains all evaluated ADE/FDE metrics within 1.2\% of a full-token HybridViT baseline using the MLQ interface and achieves comparable aggregate scores in an in-house simulation evaluation. Using XPeng Native Runtime (XNRT) on a single NVIDIA Orin-X SoC, TuringPAI-Drive generates trajectories at 12\,Hz in on-vehicle operation. For robotic manipulation, TuringPAI-Embodied achieves a 96.8\% average success rate across the four LIBERO suites. These results demonstrate a shared vision-language foundation for driving and robotic manipulation under practical on-device constraints.

all_scored.title: A four-level executable validation protocol for evaluating LLM-generated topology specifications of physics-based HVAC digital twins
all_scored.summary: Physics-based digital twins of air conditioning, a principal energy consumer in manufacturing and buildings, can be generated automatically from a declarative specification of its equipment, connections, and sizing. Large language models (LLMs) now write such specifications from plain-language descriptions. Evaluations of these specifications stop at parse success, completed runs, or textual similarity, and cannot reject a model that converges in simulation but is physically wrong. In this study, a four-level protocol is proposed that tests whether an LLM-written specification not only executes but also yields a physically valid digital twin. Each specification is executed through static validity, model build, simulation convergence, and behavioral equivalence with a hidden reference model within bands calibrated by $\pm$20% sizing perturbations. The protocol was applied to eight LLMs and fourteen HVAC topologies, five describing an existing low-humidity test chamber. To test for authorship bias, engineers and a second model family also described six topologies. Within three repairs, seven of eight models built in 98.6 to 100% of trials, with simulations converging in at least 80.0%, but reached behavioral equivalence in only 50.0 to 98.6%. About half of the failed trials converged, but not to the reference steady state, mostly in desiccant rotor systems. Pooled pass rates varied by under five percentage points across description authors. These results imply that the physics hardest to model in each field, here the desiccant rotor, must enter the generation framework as validation levels. The protocol can be adapted to other fields that generate executable digital twins from declarative specifications.

all_scored.title: Inverse ECG Reconstruction via a Preconditioned Variational Quantum Linear Solver
all_scored.summary: Inverse electrocardiography (ECG) reconstructs heart-surface potentials from body-surface measurements, enabling noninvasive mapping of cardiac electrical activity. However, the reconstruction requires solving dense and ill-conditioned linear systems, whose computational cost grows rapidly with the refined heart mesh. Quantum computing offers new opportunities for solving such systems. This paper presents a hybrid quantum-classical framework for inverse ECG reconstruction, which, to the best of our knowledge, is the first to apply a quantum linear solver to this problem. We first propose a Laplacian-regularized pre-encoding procedure to reduce the dimension of the system while improving its conditioning. Second, the resulting reduced system is encoded and solved using a coherent variational quantum linear solver (VQLS). Finally, we provide a rigorous theoretical proof establishing that the proposed framework preserves the exact solution of the original reconstruction problem throughout all stages of the computational process. Experimental results on a realistic heart-torso geometry demonstrate that our approach holds significant ability for accurate inverse ECG reconstruction. These findings highlight the potential of quantum solvers for noninvasive cardiac imaging, providing a foundation for further research into quantum-enhanced cardiac assessment and other healthcare applications.

all_scored.title: Raptor: Rejection-aware Adaptive Tree based on Speculative Decoding
all_scored.summary: Tree-structured speculative decoding accelerates vision-language models (VLMs) by verifying multiple candidate continuations in parallel. However, long visual contexts increase the cost of speculative computation, making candidate coverage and redundant expansion important considerations beyond tree topology adaptation. We propose Raptor, a training-free framework that uses rejection feedback to jointly regulate candidate coverage and drafting effort. Our key insight is that acceptance length alone cannot distinguish insufficient candidate coverage from excessive deep expansion, and these conditions require different allocation decisions. Raptor therefore extracts complementary rejection-aware signals to characterize speculative progress, frontier coverage, and redundant expansion. These signals jointly guide bounded, momentum-smoothed updates of tree depth, branching width, and drafting budget, together with execution control that limits unnecessary drafting and progressively restores expansion when appropriate. Extensive experiments with two VLMs across seven multimodal benchmarks demonstrate the effectiveness of Raptor, achieving up to 2.39x average speedup over autoregressive decoding.

all_scored.title: Evolve Where It Matters: Coverage-Guided Self-Evolution of Agent Skills
all_scored.summary: Agent skills package procedural knowledge as natural-language instructions, and a skill helps only when its instructions are correct and properly followed by the agent. Self-evolving agents revise their own skills from the runs they make, but existing methods judge each run as a whole, by its outcome or by where it went wrong, and cannot tell whether a failure comes from a wrong instruction or from one the agent did not follow. Instruction-level coverage was introduced to test skills and labels each instruction of a run as follow, not-follow, or not covered, which separates these causes. We leverage it for skill self-evolution with SkillPlumber, a framework in which an agent evolves its own skills where coverage shows they fall short. A persistent root cause analysis agent turns each label into a revision question and checks each revision against the next run, while a maintainer distills investigations across tasks into a shared strategy library. Across three benchmarks and three executors, SkillPlumber solves 64.7% to 70.5% of the tasks, 25.6 to 30.4 percentage points higher than the initial skill and 8.7 to 14.0 percentage points higher than the strongest baseline, and removing coverage reduces recovered failures by 20.8% on SkillsBench with GPT-5.5.

all_scored.title: Instance-Optimal Moment Estimation in the Add-Remove Model of Differential Privacy
all_scored.summary: In this paper, we study the problem of estimating empirical means, variances, and covariances under pure differential privacy in the add-remove model. While existing mechanisms achieve optimal worst-case error, they may not be optimal for individual datasets. To measure the performance of mechanisms on individual datasets, we introduce instance-dependent error metrics and prove sharp lower bounds on them. Then, we design mechanisms that achieve these lower bounds and demonstrate that they achieve asymptotically better utility compared to existing methods.

all_scored.title: Coordinate Basis Linear Bandits with Sublinear Regret over Low-Rank Clusters
all_scored.summary: We study the problem of computational efficiency for linear bandits in high-dimensional settings with a finite arm set. In linear bandits, the increase in the dimension $d$ of the feature vectors leads to growing computational costs of $O(d^2)$ at each round of update. Traditional low-rank approximation methods such as SOFUL reduce computation via fixed-size matrix sketching, yet run the risk of incurring vacuous linear regret when the spectral tail of the data is heavy and the approximation rank is inadequately selected. To guarantee regret convergence and effectively reduce computational costs, we introduce a clustering mechanism and propose the Coordinate Basis Linear Bandit (CBL) algorithm. Our method preserves the full covariance information in each cluster by maintaining an exact orthonormal basis of the cluster's column space together with a low-dimensional coordinate representation, which guarantees robust sublinear regret without spectral-tail vulnerabilities. It performs cluster switching by assigning a sentinel for each cluster, and reduces per-round update computation to $O(\bar r^2)$ in the cluster's effective dimension $\bar r=\min(r,l)$, where $r$ is the intrinsic rank of the data and $l<d$ is a tunable rank bound.

all_scored.title: MIR-Depth: Multi-Range Refinement for Single-View RGB-D Depth Completion of Transparent Objects
all_scored.summary: Recovering accurate visible-surface depth from a single RGB-D image and an object mask is essential for robotic grasping and manipulation of transparent objects. Specular reflections cause missing depth, while refraction corrupts nonzero returns with background depth, making raw measurements unreliable as surface anchors. Under a fixed sampling budget, refining an initial single-view prediction within a single search interval either misses large refraction offsets or sacrifices fine local resolution. To resolve this single-view trade-off, MIR-Depth constructs Coordinate-Aware Multi-Range Hypotheses: a 3D-aggregated global inverse-depth volume and depth-axis-filtered pixel-wise local volumes around a prior-guided initial depth. Selective Recurrent Refinement then introduces out-of-bounds lookup masking and validity-masked softmax fusion to iteratively update inverse depth from these volumes using a multi-scale ConvGRU. Finally, Spatially Gated Correction applies a learned per-pixel spatial gate to the full-resolution residual, preserving accurate initial geometry without imposing raw sensor readings as hard constraints. Experiments on TransCG, TODD, TRansPose, ClearPose, and HouseCat6D show that MIR-Depth achieves lower error than ReMake, DFNet, BP-Net, and PSD. Real-robot evaluations confirm accurate surface geometry for 6-DoF grasp pose prediction. Code and pretrained models will be publicly available.

all_scored.title: Antom 3-in-1 Transformer: A Payment Foundation Model
all_scored.summary: We report the development of Antom 3-in-1 Transformer, a payment foundation model that integrates sequence, tabular, and graph representations for payment risk detection. The model contains approximately 7B parameters, with approximately 1.7B activated per task route. Antom 3-in-1 Transformer is pretrained to learn reusable behavioral and relational representations, primarily on Ant International's internal payment data. In a cross-business transfer experiment, pretraining improves the target business metric by 34.5% over the same architecture trained from scratch. With only 25% of the training labels, the pretrained model outperforms the full-label scratch baseline in Average Precision (AP) and Recall@0.5% on different merchant domains. In a four-month online experiment on Ant International's billion-scale payment platform, the model reduced the overall loss rate by 37.88% relative to XGB-Online.

all_scored.title: Causal Discovery with False Positive Error Control
all_scored.summary: Causal discovery methods produce data-driven hypotheses about causal relationships, which may become new scientific findings or inform decisions about downstream interventions. In such settings, false positive causal claims can be more consequential than false negatives. Yet few methods target false positive error control in causal discovery, and existing error guarantees are often asymptotic and require strong versions of the faithfulness assumption. We introduce the $m$-conservative PC algorithm and prove that it controls false discovery rate in the linear Gaussian setting under an extremely weak version of the faithfulness assumption. In our framework, false positive error for causal graphs is defined based on the conditional-independence information they entail, yielding a metric that penalizes both false adjacencies and incorrect edge orientations. The parameter $m$ quantifies a trade-off between algorithmic complexity and the strength of the required faithfulness assumption. The $m$-conservative PC algorithm combines undirected graph learning, a Benjamini-Yekutieli-style procedure for conditional independence testing, and a conservative orientation step that marks unresolved or contradictory edge directions as ambiguous. Our algorithm produces valid outputs and retains error guarantees even in the finite-sample setting, despite possible random errors in the conditional independence tests.

all_scored.title: Differentiable Hydrodynamics for Whole-Body MPC of Underwater Robots
all_scored.summary: Underwater vehicle-manipulator systems distribute actuation across thrusters and joint motors. Whole-body model predictive control (MPC), rather than separate vehicle and arm controllers, can coordinate both to extend the workspace and exploit the system's full kinematic capability. Doing so, however, requires a hydrodynamic model and derivatives throughout the prediction horizon. Computational fluid dynamics (CFD) captures geometry-dependent forces and moments for such a model, but is too expensive to evaluate online. We present a differentiable analytical hydrodynamic model combining smooth spherical-harmonic force and moment fields with a coupled added-inertia matrix identified from CFD. It compactly represents velocity and acceleration-dependent loads and provides their derivatives in closed form. These derivatives are propagated through free-floating vehicle--manipulator dynamics for whole-body trajectory optimization and receding-horizon control, jointly optimizing thruster forces and joint torques for reaching and continuous tracking. Held-out CFD tests validate the principal translational-force and rotational-moment fields and the added-inertia response. The analytical Jacobians evaluate faster and avoid the step-size sensitivity of central finite differences. Closed-loop Stonefish experiments demonstrate whole-body MPC in an independent marine simulator. By making geometry-dependent hydrodynamics directly available to gradient-based control, the model incorporates water forces and their sensitivities into motion allocation between the vehicle and arm, rather than treating them only as disturbances.

all_scored.title: Fundamentals for Binary Classification Under Label Noise
all_scored.summary: This chapter surveys fundamental results for binary classification under label noise. Binary classification under label noise involves training models on datasets where class labels are partially incorrect, leading to degraded performance and misclassification. We distinguish poisoning attacks from noise processes and formalize random classification noise, Massart noise, and malicious classification noise within the probably approximately correct (PAC) framework. These models capture different adversarial strengths and data-generation realities. We then highlight some core ideas and representative results. In particular, we explain why random classification noise preserves the expected ordering of hypotheses and thus supports learning using the empirical risk minimization (ERM) principle, how sample complexity depends on the noise rate, and why learning algorithms often require an upper bound on the corruption level, as well as how such a bound may be estimated from data in the case of random classification noise. We also discuss computational aspects of ERM under noise and present a canonical negative result technique -- the method of induced distributions -- within the malicious noise model where the adversary has more power and may affect not only the label of an example but also the instance. We conclude with pointers to related work and a taxonomy that organizes classical label-noise models using the NCAR/NAR/NNAR lens.
